suggestions.title: 1. Swallowed Too Much?: the charcoal and poison control paragraphs, with the hour from the review they cite
suggestions.whose: the post's text, drafted by a model (no version of yours on record for either paragraph); the stance on poison control is yours
suggestions.question:
Both paragraphs as they stand read [AI Generated, High](https://www.pangram.com/history/862a4a34-aeee-4b38-921d-64db9367992b). This version reads [Human High, 200 words in one window](https://www.pangram.com/history/75a2458d-38e7-4413-8d12-9ac6f8e7824c):
"If they swallowed it within the last hour or so (slow-release pills leave a few hours more), activated charcoal may help, since it binds to a lot of drugs in the gut before the body can absorb them. It only helps with what binds to it, which leaves out alcohol and lithium among other things, and it can also adsorb medication they need. I'd only give it to somebody who's fully alert and able to swallow, because anybody who is vomiting, sedated, seizing or otherwise unable to protect their airway could breathe it into their lungs (aspiration)."
"If you're unsure charcoal would be of any value to them, poison control may be useful. They're also who to ask when you can't tell what the substance is or what it does in combination with something else they took, or when there may be a delayed risk (the worst coming hours later). I don't treat calling poison control as a mandatory ritual, though, since how useful they are varies by country and by whoever answers. And what they give you is help deciding, so go on with any first aid while you talk to them."
Three things in it are new, all from [the review the paragraph already cites](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6620762/) (Zellner and others, 2019), whose link now sits on "within the last hour or so" in place of the bare "Clinical review." label. It says to give charcoal "as soon as possible, within the first hour of the ingestion", and up to 6 hours after for timed-release preparations, which is my "slow-release pills leave a few hours more". Its list of what charcoal binds poorly or not at all has alcohols and lithium on it, along with iron and other metals, acids and bases, cyanides, and solvents, DMSO among them.
One thing the same review says against your stance: a poison control centre or a doctor should be contacted before somebody who isn't medical gives charcoal. Your "I don't treat calling poison control as a mandatory ritual" stays as you have it; tell me if you want the review's view said next to it.
Your closing line, "It is decision support, not first aid.", is said as what to do: "so go on with any first aid while you talk to them". All four cases of the warning stay (vomiting, sedated, seizing, unable to protect the airway), now with what happens to them.
In, or not?
suggestions.why: it reads Human High, but it sharpens a medical caution: the hour, the slow-release note and the two examples are not in your post, and your closing line becomes an instruction
suggestions.stays: both paragraphs as your post has them
suggestions.advice_note: in; and leave your stance on poison control as it is
